title: Everything perishes but His face
hook: all on earth passes, and the face of your Lord remains, full of majesty and honor (55:26–27)

segments.voice: Yesterday, two seas, and your line was two seas, one barrier. Where did you see two things meet and both stay themselves? Today we close Surah Ar-Rahman. Day six hundred seven.

Open the photos on your phone and scroll back ten years. The café in that picture closed. The dog is gone. The friend in the corner moved across the world. Even the phone that took the photo is in a drawer somewhere, dead. Nothing in the picture stayed exactly as it was, and you knew that even while you were taking it. In the middle of all its gifts, Surah Ar-Rahman says this out loud, in two short verses. And then it names the one thing it says does not pass.
screen: `THE CAFÉ CLOSED. THE DOG IS GONE.`

segments.voice: Verses twenty-six and twenty-seven. Pickthall: "Everyone that is thereon will pass away; There remaineth but the Countenance of thy Lord of Might and Glory." In Arabic: kullu man 'alayha fan, wa yabqa wajhu rabbika dhul-jalali wal-ikram. Fan means passing away, perishing. Yabqa means remains, stays. Two verbs, set against each other. And the one who remains is described with a phrase Muslims say often: dhul-jalali wal-ikram, Possessor of Majesty and Honor. After the five daily prayers, a hadith in Muslim records that the Prophet ﷺ would say a short line ending with exactly these words: blessed are You, Possessor of Majesty and Honor. So the phrase from this verse sits in the daily routine of millions. What does face mean here? Muslims have answered in more than one way. Many Sunni theologians affirm the face as an attribute of God, real but unlike anything created, without asking how. Others read face as God's very self, his essence. And some commentators add a third layer: what remains is whatever was done for God's face, for his sake. Surah Al-Qasas says it with the same word: everything perishes except his face. Now notice where the verses sit. Right after them comes the refrain again: which of your Lord's favors will you deny? Passing away is listed among the favors. Commentators explain it in different ways, but one reading is this: if everything here lasted forever, nothing would point beyond itself. Because things pass, they make room to notice what stays.
screen: `FAN: PASSING. YABQA: REMAINS.` · `POSSESSOR OF MAJESTY AND HONOR.` · `WHAT FACE MEANS: MORE THAN ONE READING.` · `PASSING AWAY, LISTED AS A FAVOR.`

segments.voice: The practice: hold something fleeting, gently. Pick up something near you: a cup of tea going cold, a leaf, a pen running low, your own hand. Hold it lightly. Breathe, and let yourself know it won't last, without gripping harder. If you pray, you can say quietly, ya dhal-jalali wal-ikram, O Possessor of Majesty and Honor, the words from the hadith. If not, simply hold the thing and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Everything perishes but His face. All on earth passes, and the face of your Lord remains, full of majesty and honor. Today's word.
screen: `EVERYTHING PERISHES BUT HIS FACE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: his face remains. Today, when something ends, a meal, a song, a day, let it go gently, and notice what you feel. Day six hundred seven.

howItsDone: Many Muslims say a short remembrance after each obligatory prayer that ends with 'Possessor of Majesty and Honor', and these verses of Ar-Rahman are often recited at times of loss.

original.note: Arabic: and the face of your Lord remains. yabqa, remains, set against fan, passing away.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sad verse about death.
what it means: everything passes, one remains, and even passing is counted as a favor.
what a scholar hears: wajh is read as a divine attribute (bila kayf), as God's self, or as what is done for his sake; the closing phrase reappears in the post-prayer remembrance in Sahih Muslim 591.
